latin.131: CAPUT XI. A Pelagianorum, Socinianorum, & Remonstrantium in hoc negotio sententia Placeum esse alienum. Ut nos reddat exosos, & gravissimis obruat praejudiciis, dolet nos cum Pelagianis & Socinianis paria facere. Sed dolendi causa nulla est: Nam ab hujusmodi hominum erroribus abhorremus, ut qui maxime. Vetustissimorum, addit, haereticorum (Marcionitas puto, & Manicheos, qui legem antiquam malam esse summa cum impietate afferebant) sententia fuit, nullam esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem. Quid hoc ad rem?
latin.132: Nos-ne idem cum illis haereticis sentimus? Imo eis contradicimus. Aliquam enim esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem credimus, & docemus; ipsiusque primi Adae peccati imputationem admittimus consequentem seu mediatam. Adde quod non in ea sententia, sed in dogmate, quod inde probare satagebant, absurdissimo eorum sita erat haeresis. Itaque quos duos testes laudat D. G. Origenem hom. 8. in Exod. & Hieronymum Comm. in Ezech. xviii. 1. 2. eos ambos laudat contra se. Cum enim Origenes protulisset illa verba, quae D. G. recitat — Videamus quomodo reddi dicantur peccata patrum in filios in tertiam & quartam generationem. In hoc enim sermone solent nos haeretici suggillare, quod non sit boni Dei sermo, qui pro peccatis alterius alterum plecti dicat — Respondet-ne, id quod D. G. respondisset, hoc minime esse injustum? Imo cum injustum id putaret, minimeque Deum decere, confugit ad sensum metaphoricum, & per parentes intelligi voluit Diabolum & angelos eius, per filios ac primam generationem eos quos Diabolus immediate seducit, per secundam eos qui ab his proxime seducuntur, per tertiam & quartam eos quos hi vel socios, vel administros peccati sibi adjungunt. Hos autem homines filios diaboli corripi & puniri in hoc saeculo, ut serventur: diabolorum vero, qui sunt eorum parentes, supplicium differri in futurum saeculum.
latin.133: Ad Hieronymum autem quod attinet, eius quidem ea sunt verba quae D. G. laudat. Sed quomodo nodum illum solvit? quomodo verba Decalogi, qui reddo peccata patrum super filios &c. interpretatur? Num ea, sicut D. G. de imputatione immediata accipit? Nullo modo. Scandalum, inquit ibidem, patiebamur occultum, quod injustitia videretur Dei, alium peccare, & alium luere peccata. Si enim reddit peccata patrum super filios in tertiam & quartam generationem, injustum videtur ut alius peccet & alius puniatur. Sed ex eo quod sequitur: His qui me oderunt, comminationis sive praecepti scandalum solvitur. Non enim ideo puniuntur in tertia & in quarta generatione, quia deliquerunt patres eorum: cum patres potius qui fuerunt peccatores, puniri debuerint: sed quia patrum extiterunt aemulatores & oderunt Deum, haereditario malo & impietate in ramos quoque de radice crescente. Quid potuit dici nostrae sententiae accommodatius? Habet idem Hieronymus paulo post haec verba. Scriptum est in Proverbiis: Sicut uva acerba dentibus noxia est: & fumus oculis: sic iniquitas his qui utuntur ea. Ex quo perspicuum est non aliorum dolere dentes & obstupescere, sed eorum qui uvam acerbam comederint. Est autem loci istius hic sensus: Quomodo si quis velit dicere: Patres uvam acerbam comederunt, & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt: ridiculum est, & nullam habens consequentiam: sic iniquum est atque perversum peccare patres, & filios nepotesque cruciari. Quid contra imputationem antecedentem dici potuit disertius?
latin.134: His ergo missis sibi non faventibus accedit D. G. ad Pelagianos, & miratur Aegidii Hunnii ἀτοπίαν, pertendentis hanc fuisse Pelagianorum sententiam, Adami peccatum posteris imputari. Miratur etiam hallucinatum in eadem re virum doctum (Placeum designat) ita de hoc negotio in privata quadam Epistola loquentem. Qui primi immediatam (nota immediatam: hanc enim solam, minime vero mediatam, Placeus constanter improbavit) imputationem peccati Adae commenti sunt, ii Pelagiani fuerunt, qui hac ratione conati sunt anathematum adversus Pelagium vibratorum impetum declinare. Negarunt enim corruptionem haereditariam, id est, originale peccatum: & ad praestringendos Ecclesiae oculos, hoc nomine donaverunt reatum imputati primi Adae peccati. Hoc D. G. falsum esse clamat. Fatetur tamen eos qui totam rationem peccati originalis sola imputatione peccati Adae definierunt, Pelagianis accensendos esse: sed accensendos, non quia imputationem posuerint, sed quia corruptionem negaverint, &c. Id quod Aegidii Hunnii & Placei sententiam confirmat potius quam evertit. Non enim dogma de imputatione primi peccati immediata ipsi Pelagio aut omnibus Pelagianis ascripserunt: Sed illis duntaxat, qui cum essent revera Pelagiani, voluerunt non Pelagiani videri: quam ad rem inutile fuisset dogma de imputato Adae peccato, si id Pelagius aperte protulisset. Cum enim viderent, qui negarent peccatum originale pro haereticis haberi, professi sunt se peccatum originale credere: sed hoc nomine non peccatum propagatum, ut reliqui omnes orthodoxi, sed peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputatum intelligebant. Certe illi ipsi, qui adversus Placeum imputationem immediatam urgent, imprudentes quidem, sed tamen evitare non possunt, quin Pelagianis accedant; uti jam in ipso D. Garissolio aliquoties observavi. Posito enim peccato propagato seu inhaerente, quod vere peccatum sit, ac nobis damnandis sufficiat, quid opus est alio peccato nobis imputato? posita imputatione primi Adae peccati actualis mediata, quid opus est immediata? & quomodo potest immediata ex Scriptura probari?
latin.135: Hic D. Garissolius multis verbis, ac prolatis aliquot testibus, confirmat Pelagium nullam imputationem Adamici peccati credidisse. Quorsum? nescio. Quis enim negat? An propterea Placeus paria facit cum Pelagio? Nonne Placei sententia Pelagianae contradicit apertissime? Pelagius omnem imputationem peccati Adae damnabat, Placeus non omnem, sed immediatam duntaxat. Ille nullam imputationem peccati Adae justam esse putabat, Placeus nonnullam esse arbitratur justam, nempe mediatam. Ille peccatum originale negabat, Placeus contra peccatum originale confitetur & probat. Qui tantopere opponuntur, quomodo paria facere dicuntur? At negat Pelagius imputationem immediatam, quam etiam Placeus negat. At, inquam, in ea negatione nunquam sita fuit haeresis Pelagiana. Non quicquid aut negavit, aut affirmavit Pelagius, continuo haereticum est. Percurramne illa omnia quae D. Garissolius Pelagianis tribuit § VI? Illi, inquit, 1. Justitiam originalem deperditam fuisse negabant. Placeus contra deperditam fuisse affirmat. Imo justitiam nullam originalem agnoscebat. Placeus justitiam originalem agnoscit. Sentiebant nos ut sine virtute sic sine vitio nasci. Sentit Placeus nos penitissime imbutos vitio nasci. Itaque infantes in illo statu esse in quo fuerat Adam ante praevaricationem. Itaque infantes non esse in eo statu in quo fuerat Adam ante praevaricationem, sed in multo deteriore. 2. Naturae humanae aliquam ab origine corruptionem inesse negabant. Placeus contra affirmat. 3. Necessitatem moriendi non habebant pro poena peccati, sed pro sequela & conditione naturae. Docebant enim Adamum sive peccasset, sive non peccasset, moriturum. Placeus habet necessitatem moriendi pro necessitate subeundi poenam, non autem pro sequela & conditione naturae. Docet enim Adamum, si non peccasset, non fuisse moriturum. 4. Poenis aeternis infantes ullos damnari negabant, eas quippe non aliunde quam ex propria uniuscujusque injustitia provenire. Placeus id non negat, quippe qui sciat poenas aeternas etiam ex innata injustitia provenire. Denique nullam omnino poenam propter Adae peccatum posteris irrogari putaverunt: Placeus contra aliquam poenam propter Adae peccatum posteris irrogari putat, nempe mortem. Itaque imputationem agnoscit immediatam peccati Adae habitualis propagati ac intra nos existentis, & mediatam peccati Adae actualis extra nos olim producti. Vides igitur, Lector, Placeum nullo modo esse Pelagianum: Quorsum ergo D. G. hoc loco patientia lectoris ad id probandum quod nemo negat, Pelagium negasse imputationem peccati Adami, abutitur, ejusque errores enumerat, quasi illorum Placeus esset particeps?
latin.136: Interim quia obiter laudat ex Augustini opere imperfecto contra secundam Juliani responsionem Lutetiae edito anno hujus saeculi decimo septimo, locum, Qui, inquit, vel solus, si alius non extaret apud Augustinum, satis docet quid de hac imputatione & ipse & Ecclesia Catholica senserit, eum locum inspiciamus: Augustinus enim, si sibi constat, totus noster est. Quid est ergo quod clamas & dicis non posse Deum & dimittere peccata majoribus propter propria, & imputare parvulis aliena. (Videtur & delenda vox propter inutilis eo loco & incommoda, & sententia alio quodam mendo laborare. Non dicebat enim Julianus Deum non posse majoribus, hoc est, adultis propria dimittere peccata; sed dicebat non decere Deum, qui dimittit peccata majoribus propria, imputare parvulis aliena.) Nec vis attendere quod nonnisi in Christo renatis, utraque; non renatis autem in Christo neutra dimittantur. Ipsa sunt enim Christiana & gratiae sacramenta abscondita sapientibus & prudentibus & revelata parvulis. In quibus, o si esses, nec quasi magnus in tua virtute consideres, profecto intelligeres, sic imputari generatis parvulis injustitiam primi hominis ad subeundum supplicium, quemadmodum imputatur parvulis regeneratis justitia secundi hominis ad obtinendum regnum coelorum. Nobis hic locus minime nocet. Imputationem enim intelligit, quae generationem, atque adeo ingenitam corruptionem sequitur; cum imputatio, quam negamus, ut corruptionem sic generationem antecedere putetur; causa enim creditur esse, cur gignamur corrupti. Adde quod nihil prohibet per injustitiam primi hominis, injustitiam intelligere habitualem, quam ad parvulos primus homo per generationem transmisit. Certe enim cum Augustino objiceretur a Pelagianis, Qui fieri possit, ut Deus, qui pro sua bonitate nostra ipsorum peccata remittit, velit imputare aliena? Respondit, teste Martyre, Deum summe bonum esse, neque, quod isti assumunt, in culpa originis imputare nobis alienum peccatum, sed nostram ipsorum iniquitatem, quae nostrae naturae adhaeret jam inde ab ipsa origine. Addam aliud ejusdem Martyris de Augustino testimonium. Augustinus, inquit, in Enchiridio ad Laurentium capite 46. probabile ait esse, peccata etiam proximorum parentum communicari cum filiis. Ad quod probandum componit inter se duo loca Scripturarum a nobis ante tractata: Quod Deus ait, se velle persequi peccata patrum in filios in tertiam, & quartam generationem: quum alio loco dicat, Filium non portaturum iniquitatem patris. Si filius, inquit, non portat iniquitatem patris, sed suam, & tamen Deus persequitur in eo peccatum patris, oportet, ut filius ipse peccatum illud in se habeat: Alioqui haec loca inter se non convenirent. Num haec dixisset Augustinus, si peccati paterni imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam credidisset, qua scilicet filius sit peccator & reus, alioqui non peccator, nec reus?
latin.137: De Socinianis, cum nihil differant a Pelagianis, quid opus est dicere? Ad Arminianos autem quod spectat, ab eorum etiam erroribus, Dei beneficio, abhorret Placeus. Qui autem pro Clariss. Molineo Respondit Corvino doctissimus Walaeus, is non dubitavit imputationem immediatam disertis verbis negare, uti a nobis observatum est supra, pag. 22. nec propterea partibus Remonstrantium favere existimatur. Atque haec fuerunt argumenta D. Garissolii.

pass_a.131: Chapter XI. That Placeus is foreign to the opinion of the Pelagians, Socinians, and Remonstrants in this matter. So that he may render us hated and overwhelm us with the heaviest prejudices, it grieves him that we make common cause with the Pelagians and Socinians. But there is no cause for grieving: for we shrink from the errors of such men as much as anyone. He adds that the opinion of the most ancient heretics (I take it the Marcionites and the Manichees, who with the height of impiety asserted that the ancient law was evil) was that there can be no just imputation of another's sin. What does this have to do with the matter?
pass_a.132: Do we hold the same as those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. For we believe and teach that there can be some just imputation of another's sin; and we admit the imputation of the first Adam's own sin as consequent or mediate. Add that their heresy was situated not in that opinion, but in the most absurd dogma they were busy proving from it. Therefore the two witnesses Lord Garissoles praises — Origen, Homily 8 on Exodus, and Jerome's Commentary on Ezekiel 18:1–2 — he praises both against himself. For when Origen had brought forward those words which Garissoles quotes — Let us see how the sins of the fathers are said to be visited on the sons into the third and fourth generation. For in this saying heretics are accustomed to taunt us, that it is not the speech of a good God who says another is punished for another's sins — Does Origen answer what Garissoles would have answered, that this is by no means unjust? No: since he thought it unjust and wholly unbecoming to God, he fled to a metaphorical sense, and wanted the parents to be understood as the Devil and his angels, the sons and first generation as those the Devil immediately seduces, the second as those next seduced by these, the third and fourth as those whom these join to themselves as partners or servants of sin. But these men, sons of the devil, are seized and punished in this age that they may be saved; yet the punishment of the demons who are their parents is deferred to the age to come.
pass_a.133: As for Jerome, those are indeed his words which Garissoles praises. But how does he untie that knot? How does he interpret the Decalogue's words, 'I visit the sins of the fathers upon the sons,' and so on? Does he take them, as Garissoles does, of immediate imputation? By no means. We were suffering, he says in the same place, a hidden scandal — that God's injustice seemed to be that one sins and another pays for the sins. For if He visits the fathers' sins on the sons into the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished. But from what follows — 'to those who hate Me' — the scandal of the threat or precept is solved. For they are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned (rather the fathers who were sinners ought to have been punished), but because they proved imitators of their fathers and hated God, with hereditary evil and impiety growing into the branches also from the root. What could be said more fitted to our opinion? The same Jerome a little later has these words. It is written in Proverbs: As sour grapes are harmful to the teeth, and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who use it. From which it is clear that not others' teeth ache and go numb, but those of the ones who ate the sour grapes. And the sense of that place is this: Just as if someone should say, 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the sons' teeth went numb,' that is ridiculous and has no consequence, so it is unjust and perverse that fathers sin and sons and grandsons are tortured. What could be said more plainly against antecedent imputation?
pass_a.134: So, setting aside these witnesses who do not favor him, Garissoles turns to the Pelagians, and wonders at Aegidius Hunnius's ἀτοπία (absurdity), who contended that this was the Pelagians' opinion — that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity. He also wonders that a learned man (he means Placeus) hallucinated in the same matter, speaking thus about this business in a certain private Letter. Those who first invented the immediate imputation of Adam's sin (note: immediate — for this alone, and by no means the mediate, Placeus has constantly rejected) were Pelagians, who by this device tried to dodge the force of the anathemas hurled against Pelagius. For they denied hereditary corruption, that is, original sin; and to dazzle the Church's eyes they honored with that name the guilt of Adam's first sin imputed. Garissoles cries that this is false. Yet he admits that those who defined the whole account of original sin by the sole imputation of Adam's sin are to be classed with the Pelagians — classed not because they posited imputation, but because they denied corruption, and so on. That confirms Hunnius's and Placeus's opinion rather than overturns it. For they did not ascribe the dogma of immediate imputation of the first sin to Pelagius himself or to all Pelagians, but only to those who, while truly Pelagians, wanted not to seem Pelagians — for which purpose the dogma of Adam's sin imputed would have been useless if Pelagius had openly put it forward. For when they saw that those who denied original sin were held for heretics, they professed to believe original sin; but by that name they understood not propagated sin, as all the rest of the orthodox, but Adam's actual sin imputed to all. Certainly those very ones who urge immediate imputation against Placeus, though unwittingly, still cannot avoid coming near the Pelagians — as I have already observed several times in Garissoles himself. For once a propagated or inherent sin is granted that is truly sin and enough to damn us, what need is there of another sin imputed to us? Once mediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin is granted, what need of the immediate? And how can the immediate be proved from Scripture?
pass_a.135: Here Lord Garissoles, with many words and some witnesses brought forward, confirms that Pelagius believed no imputation of Adam's sin. To what end? I do not know. For who denies it? Does Placeus therefore make common cause with Pelagius? Does not Placeus's opinion contradict the Pelagian one most openly? Pelagius condemned every imputation of Adam's sin; Placeus not every, but only the immediate. That one thought no imputation of Adam's sin just; Placeus judges some to be just, namely the mediate. That one denied original sin; Placeus on the contrary confesses and proves original sin. Who are so greatly opposed — how are they said to make common cause? But Pelagius denies immediate imputation, which Placeus also denies. Yet, I say, the Pelagian heresy was never situated in that denial. Not whatever Pelagius denied or affirmed is at once heretical. Shall I run through all those things Garissoles attributes to the Pelagians in section VI? They, he says, 1. denied that original justice had been lost. Placeus on the contrary affirms it was lost. Indeed Pelagius acknowledged no original justice at all. Placeus acknowledges original justice. They held that we are born as without virtue so without vice. Placeus holds that we are born steeped most deeply in vice. So they: infants are in that state in which Adam was before the fall. So Placeus: infants are not in that state in which Adam was before the fall, but in one much worse. 2. They denied that any corruption from the origin is in human nature. Placeus affirms the contrary. 3. They did not take the necessity of dying as the penalty of sin, but as a sequel and condition of nature. For they taught that Adam would have died whether he had sinned or not. Placeus takes the necessity of dying as the necessity of undergoing penalty, not as a sequel and condition of nature. For he teaches that Adam, if he had not sinned, would not have died. 4. They denied that any infants are damned with eternal penalties, since those come from nowhere but each one's own injustice. Placeus does not deny that, since he knows eternal penalties also come from innate injustice. Finally they thought no penalty at all is inflicted on posterity because of Adam's sin; Placeus on the contrary thinks some penalty is inflicted on posterity because of Adam's sin, namely death. So he acknowledges immediate imputation of Adam's habitual sin propagated and existing within us, and mediate imputation of Adam's actual sin once produced outside us. You see then, Reader, that Placeus is in no way a Pelagian. Why then does Garissoles in this place abuse the reader's patience to prove what no one denies — that Pelagius denied the imputation of Adam's sin — and enumerate his errors as if Placeus shared in them?
pass_a.136: Meanwhile, because in passing he praises a place from Augustine's unfinished work against Julian's second reply, published at Paris in the seventeenth year of this century — a place which, he says, even alone, if no other existed in Augustine, sufficiently teaches what both he and the Catholic Church thought about this imputation — let us inspect that place: for Augustine, if he is consistent with himself, is wholly ours. What then is this that you cry and say — that God cannot both forgive adults their own sins and impute to little ones another's? (The word 'propter' also seems deletable as useless and awkward in that place, and the sentence labors under some other fault. For Julian was not saying God cannot forgive adults their own sins; he was saying it does not become God, who forgives adults their own sins, to impute to little ones another's.) Nor will you attend to this: that only to those reborn in Christ are both forgiven; but to those not reborn in Christ, neither. For the Christian sacraments of grace themselves are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones. In which, O if you were, and did not regard yourself as great in your own virtue, you would surely understand that the first man's injustice is so imputed to little ones as generated, for undergoing punishment, as the second man's justice is imputed to little ones as regenerated, for obtaining the kingdom of heaven. This place does us no harm at all. For he understands an imputation which follows generation, and so inborn corruption; whereas the imputation we deny is thought to precede generation as it does corruption — for it is believed to be the cause why we are born corrupt. Add that nothing prevents taking 'the first man's injustice' as habitual injustice, which the first man transmitted to little ones by generation. For certainly when the Pelagians objected to Augustine, How can it be that God, who in His goodness remits our own sins, should will to impute another's? He answered, as Martyr witnesses, that God is supremely good, and does not, as they assume, in the guilt of origin impute to us another's sin, but our own iniquity, which already clings to our nature from the origin itself. I will add another testimony of the same Martyr about Augustine. Augustine, he says, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 46, says it is probable that even the nearest parents' sins are shared with the children. To prove which he sets side by side two Scripture places we treated earlier: that God says He wills to pursue the fathers' sins on the sons into the third and fourth generation, while elsewhere He says the son shall not bear the father's iniquity. If the son, he says, does not bear the father's iniquity but his own, and yet God pursues in him the father's sin, the son himself must have that sin in himself: otherwise these places would not agree. Would Augustine have said this if he had believed an antecedent or immediate imputation of the father's sin, by which the son would be sinner and guilty who otherwise would be neither sinner nor guilty?
pass_a.137: Concerning the Socinians, since they differ in nothing from the Pelagians, what need is there to speak? As for the Arminians, by God's kindness Placeus shrinks from their errors also. And the most learned Walaeus, who answered Corvinus on behalf of the most distinguished Du Moulin, did not hesitate to deny immediate imputation in express words, as we noted above at page 22, and is not on that account thought to favor the Remonstrant party. And these were Lord Garissoles's arguments.

131: Chapter XI. That Placeus stands apart from the Pelagian, Socinian, and Remonstrant teaching on this question. Garissoles wants to make us hated and crush us under the heaviest prejudices by grieving that we make common cause with Pelagians and Socinians. There is nothing to grieve over. We shrink from the errors of such men as strongly as anyone can. He adds that the oldest heretics — I take him to mean the Marcionites and the Manichees, who with the height of impiety called the old law evil — held that there can be no just imputation of another's sin. What does that have to do with our question?
132: Do we agree with those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. We believe and teach that some just imputation of another's sin is possible, and we admit the imputation of Adam's first sin as consequent or mediate. Their heresy did not sit in that opinion, but in the absurd dogma they tried to prove from it. So the two witnesses Garissoles cites — Origen's eighth homily on Exodus, and Jerome on Ezekiel 18:1–2 — he cites against himself. When Origen had offered the words Garissoles quotes — how the fathers' sins are said to be visited on the children to the third and fourth generation, a saying heretics use to taunt us as unworthy of a good God who punishes one for another's sins — does Origen answer as Garissoles would, that this is not unjust at all? No. Thinking it unjust and unfit for God, he fled to metaphor: the 'parents' are the Devil and his angels; the first generation, those the Devil seduces directly; the second, those next seduced by them; the third and fourth, those they recruit as partners or servants of sin. Those human sons of the devil are seized and punished in this age so they may be saved; the demons who are their parents have their punishment deferred to the age to come.
133: As for Jerome, Garissoles does quote his words — but how does Jerome untie the knot? How does he read the Decalogue's 'I visit the fathers' sins on the children'? Does he take it, as Garissoles does, of immediate imputation? Not at all. In the same place Jerome says they were suffering a hidden scandal: it looked like God's injustice that one should sin and another pay. If God visits the fathers' sins on the children to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one sins and another is punished. But the words that follow — 'to those who hate Me' — clear the scandal. They are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned (the sinful fathers themselves ought to have been punished), but because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God, hereditary evil and impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. What could fit our view more closely? A little later Jerome cites Proverbs: as sour grapes hurt the teeth and smoke the eyes, so iniquity hurts those who use it — so it is plain that not other people's teeth ache, but the teeth of those who ate the sour grapes. The point of the place is: saying 'the fathers ate sour grapes and the sons' teeth went numb' is ridiculous and follows nothing; so it is unjust and twisted that fathers sin and sons and grandsons are tormented. What could be said more plainly against antecedent imputation?
134: Setting aside those unhelpful witnesses, Garissoles turns to the Pelagians and marvels at Aegidius Hunnius's ἀτοπία — Hunnius's claim that the Pelagian view was that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity. He also marvels that a learned man (he means Placeus) 'hallucinated' the same way in a private letter. Those who first invented the immediate imputation of Adam's sin — note: immediate; Placeus has always rejected that alone, never the mediate — were Pelagians trying to dodge the anathemas aimed at Pelagius. They denied hereditary corruption, that is, original sin, and to dazzle the Church they gave that name to the guilt of Adam's first sin as imputed. Garissoles cries that this is false; yet he admits that anyone who makes the whole account of original sin nothing but the imputation of Adam's sin belongs with the Pelagians — not because they taught imputation, but because they denied corruption. That confirms Hunnius and Placeus more than it overturns them. They never pinned immediate imputation of the first sin on Pelagius himself or on every Pelagian, but only on those who were truly Pelagians and wanted not to look it — for if Pelagius had openly taught imputed Adam's sin, that dodge would have been useless. Seeing that deniers of original sin were counted heretics, they professed to believe original sin, but meant by it not propagated sin, as all the orthodox do, but Adam's actual sin imputed to everyone. Indeed those who press immediate imputation against Placeus cannot help sliding toward the Pelagians, as I have already noted more than once in Garissoles himself: once a propagated, inherent sin that is truly sin and enough to damn us is granted, what need is there of another sin imputed to us? Once mediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin is granted, what need of the immediate — and how can Scripture prove it?
135: Here Garissoles, at length and with several witnesses, confirms that Pelagius believed in no imputation of Adam's sin. To what end? I do not know. Who denies it? Does that make Placeus Pelagius's ally? Placeus's teaching contradicts the Pelagian one as plainly as can be. Pelagius condemned every imputation of Adam's sin; Placeus condemns only the immediate. Pelagius thought no imputation of Adam's sin just; Placeus holds some just — namely the mediate. Pelagius denied original sin; Placeus confesses and proves it. How can people so opposed be said to make common cause? Yes, Pelagius denies immediate imputation, and so does Placeus — but the Pelagian heresy never sat in that denial. Not everything Pelagius denied or affirmed is heresy by that fact alone. Shall I run through all Garissoles pins on the Pelagians in section VI? (1) They denied that original justice was lost; Placeus affirms it was. Pelagius acknowledged no original justice at all; Placeus does. They held we are born without virtue and without vice; Placeus holds we are born steeped in vice. So for them infants stand where Adam stood before the fall; for Placeus infants stand in a far worse state. (2) They denied any corruption in human nature from the start; Placeus affirms it. (3) They took the necessity of dying not as sin's penalty but as nature's sequel and condition — Adam would have died whether he sinned or not; Placeus takes dying as undergoing penalty, and teaches that Adam would not have died had he not sinned. (4) They denied that any infants are damned with eternal penalties, since those come only from each one's own injustice; Placeus does not deny eternal penalties, knowing they also arise from innate injustice. Finally they thought no penalty at all is laid on posterity for Adam's sin; Placeus thinks some is — namely death. So he owns immediate imputation of Adam's habitual sin as propagated and present in us, and mediate imputation of Adam's actual sin once done outside us. Reader, Placeus is no Pelagian. Why then does Garissoles waste the reader's patience proving what no one denies — that Pelagius denied Adam's sin's imputation — and list Pelagius's errors as if Placeus shared them?
136: Meanwhile Garissoles casually praises a passage from Augustine's unfinished work against Julian's second reply (Paris, in the seventeenth year of this century) — a passage which, he says, even alone would show what Augustine and the Catholic Church thought about this imputation. Let us look at it: if Augustine is consistent, he is wholly ours. What then is this cry — that God cannot both forgive adults their own sins and impute another's to little ones? (The word propter also looks deletable there as useless and awkward, and the sentence has some other fault. Julian was not saying God cannot forgive adults their own sins; he was saying it does not become the God who forgives adults their own to impute another's to little ones.) Nor will you face this: only those reborn in Christ have both forgiven; those not reborn in Christ have neither. The Christian sacraments of grace are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones. If you were among them, and did not think yourself great in your own virtue, you would see that the first man's injustice is imputed to little ones as generated, for undergoing punishment, just as the second man's justice is imputed to little ones as regenerated, for obtaining the kingdom of heaven. That place does not hurt us. Augustine means an imputation that follows generation — and so inborn corruption — whereas the imputation we deny is supposed to precede generation as it does corruption, as if it were the cause of our being born corrupt. Nothing stops us taking 'the first man's injustice' as habitual injustice transmitted to little ones by generation. When the Pelagians asked Augustine how God, who in His goodness remits our own sins, could will to impute another's, he answered (Martyr witnesses) that God is supremely good and does not, as they assume, impute another's sin to us in the guilt of origin, but our own iniquity, which already clings to our nature from the origin itself. Martyr adds another witness: in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 46, Augustine says it is probable that even the nearest parents' sins are shared with the children. To prove it he sets together two Scriptures we already treated: God will pursue the fathers' sins on the children to the third and fourth generation, yet elsewhere the son shall not bear the father's iniquity. If the son does not bear the father's iniquity but his own, and yet God pursues the father's sin in him, the son must have that sin in himself — otherwise the places would not agree. Would Augustine have said that if he had believed an antecedent or immediate imputation of the father's sin, by which a son would be sinner and guilty who otherwise would be neither?
137: As for the Socinians, since they differ not at all from the Pelagians, what more is there to say? As for the Arminians, by God's kindness Placeus shrinks from their errors too. The learned Walaeus, answering Corvinus for the distinguished Du Moulin, did not hesitate to deny immediate imputation in plain words — as we noted above at page 22 — and is not for that reason thought to side with the Remonstrants. And those were Lord Garissoles's arguments.
